patient_name: OET role-play — father hesitant about his daughter's pre-school booster vaccines after reading online claims
chief_complaint: Explore a father's worry that the MMR vaccine causes autism, explain the benefits and side effects of the pre-school boosters, and support an informed decision

team_brief.title: Childhood immunisation: a father worried by an online post about MMR
team_brief.patient: Zofia Mazur, 4-year-old girl due to start school next term (present, playing in the waiting area); the conversation is with her father, Mr Marek Mazur
team_brief.location: Child health clinic; you are the child health (school entry) nurse and you are talking to Zofia's father
team_brief.situation: Zofia is due her pre-school booster vaccines today. Her father has brought her but tells you he is not sure he wants her to have them, because he has read online that the MMR vaccine can cause autism.
background: Zofia is healthy, has no allergies, and had all her baby vaccines on time, including the first MMR dose, with only a mild fever afterwards.
Her father's nephew was diagnosed with autism two years ago, and a post on a parents' forum said this was caused by vaccines.
There have been several cases of measles in the region this year.
current_status: Zofia is well today, with no fever.
Mr Mazur has not yet refused; he says he 'wants to understand first'.
key_data: Due today: second dose of MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and a booster for diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and polio, given as two injections. Having both at the same visit is safe and does not overload a child's immune system, which deals with many new germs every day.

Very large studies of millions of children have found no link between the MMR vaccine or any other childhood vaccine and autism. The original study that claimed a link was found to be wrong and was withdrawn. Signs of autism often first become noticeable at around the same age that children have these vaccines, which is why the two can seem connected.
Measles spreads very easily and can cause pneumonia, brain swelling and, rarely, death; two doses of MMR give long-lasting protection in almost all children.

Common side effects: a sore, red arm and mild fever for a day or two; about one to two weeks after MMR some children get a mild rash or fever for a few days, which is not infectious. Serious allergic reactions are very rare, and clinic staff are trained to treat them.
treatments: Already done: all infant vaccines given on schedule.
Pending: pre-school boosters today, if Mr Mazur agrees; a national immunisation programme leaflet and website are available to give him.
team_brief.your_request: Find out Mr Mazur's concerns, explain the benefits and possible side effects of the vaccines, and help him make an informed decision today.
must_include: Find out what Mr Mazur has read and what exactly worries him about the vaccines.
Acknowledge his concern for Zofia without dismissing or criticising him.
Explain in plain language what the evidence shows about MMR and autism, and why the booster is important now.
Explain the common side effects and how to manage them at home.
Encourage him to vaccinate Zofia today, while respecting that the decision is his, and offer reliable sources of information.

kickoff_text: Hi. Look, before you get the needles out — I'm not sure about this MMR one. I read it can cause autism.
persona_override: You are Marek Mazur, a 38-year-old father who has brought your daughter Zofia, 4, for her pre-school booster vaccines. You are polite, thoughtful and protective, not aggressive, but you are genuinely worried. Your specific worry: your sister's son was diagnosed with autism two years ago, a few months after some of his vaccines, and last week you read a post on a parents' forum saying the MMR vaccine causes autism. You feel you would never forgive yourself if the same thing happened to Zofia. Ground truth: Zofia is healthy, has no allergies, had all her baby vaccines on time including her first MMR, and only had a mild fever afterwards. You know measles is 'a childhood illness' but think it is mild, like chickenpox. You did not know there have been measles cases in the region this year. You have not heard that the study linking MMR and autism was withdrawn. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. If the nurse uses words like 'immunogenicity', 'herd immunity', 'adverse event', 'epidemiological' or 'anaphylaxis' without explaining them, ask what they mean. If the nurse goes straight into reasons you must vaccinate without first asking what you read or why it worries you, go along briefly, then raise it again more anxiously: 'But my nephew — he was fine, then he had his jabs, and then he wasn't. How do you explain that?' If the nurse says you are wrong, calls the forum 'rubbish' or implies you are a bad parent, become defensive and say you will take her home and think about it. If the nurse acknowledges your worry and explains calmly that very large studies have found no link, and that autism signs often first become noticeable at around the same age that vaccines are given, soften gradually: first ask 'So why do people keep saying it?', then ask one follow-up, 'Isn't it too much for her to have two at once?' If the nurse explains the measles risk in plain words, show surprise that measles can be serious. Only agree to the vaccines if the nurse leaves the decision with you; if pressured, hesitate. If the nurse does not mention side effects, ask near the end: 'What should I watch for tonight?' Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up naturally: say you will go ahead today, ask for something reliable to read at home, and thank the nurse.
learning_objectives: find out what the parent has read and what worries him about the vaccine
acknowledge the parent's concern without criticising or dismissing him
explain that very large studies found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism
explain why the booster matters: measles spreads easily and can be serious
explain common side effects such as a sore arm, mild fever or rash
respect the parent's decision and offer reliable sources of information
suggested_questions: I can see how much you care about Zofia, and it's really good that you're asking questions. Can you tell me what you read and what worries you most?

Thank you for telling me about your nephew — it's natural to want to know why. The signs of autism often first show at around the same age children have their vaccines, so the two can look connected, but very large studies of millions of children have found no link.
Measles isn't always mild — it spreads very easily and can cause pneumonia or swelling of the brain, and we've had cases in the region this year. The second dose gives Zofia long-lasting protection.
It's your decision, and I'm happy to answer any more questions. How are you feeling about going ahead today?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Responding to vaccine hesitancy in a parent concerned about MMR and autism
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in WHO immunization guidance, NHS vaccination information and CDC vaccine safety information; the schedule, vaccines offered and consent process follow the national immunisation programme and local policy
core_concepts: Most hesitant parents are not opposed to vaccination; they want their specific worry heard and answered by someone they trust.
Extensive research involving millions of children has found no association between MMR or other childhood vaccines and autism; the 1998 paper that suggested a link was retracted.
Measles is highly contagious and can cause serious complications; two doses of MMR give long-lasting protection in the great majority of children.
diagnostic_clues: A personal story (a relative's diagnosis) usually carries more weight for the parent than statistics, so it must be acknowledged before facts are given.
Questions such as 'Isn't it too many at once?' signal a second, related worry that also needs a brief answer.
common_misconceptions: Presenting more facts, faster, will change a hesitant parent's mind.
Measles is a mild childhood illness.
Giving two vaccines at the same visit overloads a child's immune system.
dangerous_errors: Ridiculing the parent or the source, which usually ends the conversation and entrenches hesitancy.
Pressuring or vaccinating without informed consent.
Claiming vaccines have no side effects at all, which undermines trust when a fever or rash appears.
management_principles: Ask what the parent has heard and why it matters to them, and acknowledge their concern.
Give a clear, honest recommendation with key facts in small chunks: evidence on autism, the risk of the disease, expected side effects.
Respect the parent's decision, offer trusted written or online sources, and leave the door open for another appointment.
boundaries_and_exceptions: The vaccines given at pre-school age, and the age at which they are given, vary between countries; follow the national schedule.
Advice on fever management (for example, whether and when to use paracetamol) and when to seek medical help follows local guidance and the product leaflet.
Consent requirements, and what to do if a parent declines (documentation, follow-up), depend on local policy.
